Here are some of the most common questions to help you get started. What is 360 feedback software? 360 feedback software is a tool that collects structured performance input from an employee's manager, peers, and direct reports simultaneously, providing a complete multi-source view of how they work and lead. It replaces informal peer feedback with a consistent, anonymized process that surfaces insights no single-reviewer assessment can provide. How does 360 feedback software work in practice? 360 feedback software works by selecting a group of reviewers for each employee, sending them structured feedback forms, collecting responses anonymously, and presenting results in a consolidated report. PerformSpark manages the entire process automatically, from reviewer invitations and reminders through to final report generation for the employee and their manager. What is the difference between 360 feedback and a standard performance review? A standard performance review is completed by the direct manager alone, giving a single-perspective assessment. 360 feedback collects input from multiple sources simultaneously, including peers and direct reports, providing a fuller picture of how an employee performs and collaborates. Most organizations use both as complementary parts of their review cycle. How can 360 feedback software support reviewer confidentiality? Depending on configuration, 360 feedback software can aggregate responses and control how reviewer identities are displayed. PerformSpark supports role-based permissions and configurable workflows so organizations can choose an approach that fits their feedback policy while preserving useful multi-source input. How often should organizations run 360 feedback cycles? Most organizations run 360 feedback cycles annually or biannually, timed to align with performance reviews or leadership development programs. PerformSpark lets HR configure cycle frequency by role or seniority level so senior leaders receive more frequent multi-source feedback than individual contributors, without creating process overhead for the whole organization. What should a 360 feedback questionnaire include? A 360 feedback questionnaire should include competency-based rating questions covering areas like communication, collaboration, leadership, and delivery, alongside open-text questions asking for specific examples of strengths and areas for development. PerformSpark provides customizable templates so HR can tailor questions to match their competency framework and company values. How does 360 feedback software support leadership development? 360 feedback software supports leadership development by giving leaders a structured, multi-source view of how their behavior impacts their team. PerformSpark connects 360 results directly to individual development plans so insights from peer and direct report feedback translate into specific growth actions with timelines and manager check-ins built in. Can 360 feedback software integrate with performance reviews and goal tracking? Yes, PerformSpark connects 360 feedback results directly to performance reviews and individual development plans, so multi-source insights inform the formal review conversation rather than sitting in a separate report that gets forgotten. Managers can reference 360 themes when writing review assessments, making evaluations more balanced and evidence-based. Ready to make multi-source feedback actionable? A useful self-evaluation usually includes: Review-period and role context Major accomplishments Progress against agreed goals Feedback received and applied Challenges or incomplete work Strengths demonstrated One or two development priorities Next-period goals and support needed Use reliable evidence. Replace bracketed details in the examples with information from work records, check-ins, project reviews, customer feedback, or other approved sources. How to Use These Examples Select an example with a similar role or situation. Replace general wording with the employee's actual work. Add evidence that the manager can verify. Remove sections that do not apply. Check that team outcomes and individual contribution are distinguished. End with a useful next step or support request. Do not submit a sample unchanged. Generic language reduces the value of the self-evaluation and may conflict with the employee's actual performance record. 1. HR Leader: Exceeding Expectations “During this review period, I led the redesign of our performance review process. I mapped the existing workflow, removed duplicate approval steps, coordinated testing with managers from different departments, and created new guidance for employees and reviewers. The first cycle using the revised process had fewer access and assignment questions, and HR could monitor completion without maintaining a separate tracker. My strongest contribution was translating policy requirements into a workflow managers could use. In the next period, I want to improve how we measure review quality after completion, not only whether the forms were submitted.” 2. HR Leader: Meeting Expectations “I managed the review calendar, supported managers, prepared calibration materials, and completed the required process reporting. I responded consistently to questions and escalated sensitive cases to the appropriate HR leader. One area I want to improve is post-cycle communication. Several managers needed additional clarification about development follow-up, so I am creating a standard closeout checklist and will review its use after the next cycle.” 3. Software Engineer: Exceeding Expectations “I delivered the agreed feature scope and also addressed a recurring reliability issue that affected dependent teams. I documented the technical options, coordinated the change with platform and quality partners, and created monitoring guidance for future incidents. The work improved the team's ability to identify the issue earlier and reduced repeated investigation. I also supported two engineers through design and code reviews. My next development priority is leading a full technical design review independently, including risks, alternatives, and implementation stages.” 4. Software Engineer: Meeting Expectations “I completed the main commitments in my current goal plan and contributed consistently to code reviews and team planning. I raised dependencies when I identified them and corrected defects within the agreed process. I need to improve the clarity of my design documentation. Feedback from recent reviews showed that some assumptions were explained verbally but not written. I have started using the team's design checklist and will ask a senior engineer to review my next two documents before the formal meeting.” 5. Sales Representative: Exceeding Expectations “I achieved the agreed sales outcome for the review period and contributed beyond my assigned opportunities by documenting objections and competitive questions that appeared repeatedly in customer conversations. I worked with marketing and product teams to turn those observations into an updated enablement resource. I also supported a new team member during call preparation. My next goal is to improve forecasting consistency by documenting decision criteria, dependencies, and next actions more clearly for every active opportunity.” 6. Sales Representative: Development Needed “I did not achieve the full target for this period. The main gap was not activity volume but the quality of opportunity qualification. Several opportunities remained active without clear decision criteria or an agreed next step. I should have raised these concerns earlier and focused my time on better-qualified accounts. I have reviewed the qualification framework with my manager, will use it in every discovery conversation, and will discuss selected opportunity notes during our weekly 1-on-1.” 7. Customer Success Manager: Exceeding Expectations “I maintained clear success plans for my assigned customers and identified several material risks before they affected renewal discussions. For each risk, I documented the evidence, owner, response, and next review date, then coordinated action with the relevant internal team. I also created a reusable customer handoff checklist after noticing recurring gaps in implementation records. My next development priority is executive communication, particularly presenting customer risk and recommended action more concisely.” 8. Customer Success Manager: Development Needed “My customer relationships remained constructive, but I was not consistent in documenting risks and follow-up actions in the approved system. This made it harder for partner teams to understand the current status when I was unavailable. I have moved active risks into the shared workflow, added an owner and review date, and will review the record with my manager during each check-in until the habit is consistent.” 9. Finance Analyst: Exceeding Expectations “I completed the required reporting and identified a recurring reconciliation issue that was creating avoidable review work. I traced the difference to the source process, documented the control gap, and worked with the process owner to test a correction. The updated workflow gives reviewers a clearer record of the source, adjustment, and approval. I want to build stronger executive communication by presenting analysis as a decision, key evidence, risks, and recommendation rather than leading with technical detail.” 10. Finance Analyst: Meeting Expectations “I delivered my scheduled reports accurately and raised questions when source information was incomplete. I also supported the annual planning process by documenting assumptions and changes. Feedback indicated that my analysis is reliable but sometimes arrives too close to the decision deadline. I am improving the work plan by identifying dependencies earlier and setting internal review dates before the final due date.” 11. Operations Specialist: Meeting Expectations “I managed the assigned operational workflow, resolved exceptions, and maintained the required service and quality records. I also mapped a recurring handoff problem and proposed a limited pilot to test a clearer owner and escalation step. The pilot is still in progress, so I am not treating the result as complete. During the next period, I will review the outcome, document what changed, and recommend whether the process should be expanded or revised.” 12. Healthcare or Frontline Employee: Meeting Expectations “I completed my assigned responsibilities, followed required procedures, and raised safety or service concerns through the approved process. I contributed to team handoffs by using the standard checklist and confirming unresolved actions with the incoming employee. One area I am developing is communication during high-volume periods. I have asked my manager to observe one handoff and provide specific feedback on clarity, prioritization, and escalation.” Employees in regulated or clinical environments should adapt the wording to their role, policy, professional standards, and approved documentation process. 13. First-Time Manager: Exceeding Expectations “I established a regular check-in structure with each direct report, clarified current goals, and documented employee and manager actions. I used feedback from my own manager to ask more open questions instead of moving immediately to a solution. Team members began bringing risks and support needs earlier, which gave us more time to respond. My next development priority is delegation. I want to define outcomes and decision authority more clearly while avoiding unnecessary control of the employee's approach.” 14. People Manager: Development Needed “I delivered the team's main work commitments, but I was not consistent in providing timely individual feedback. I relied too heavily on project meetings and did not create enough space for employee development conversations. I have scheduled recurring check-ins, added feedback and development to the agenda, and will track the commitments I make to each employee. I will review this progress with my manager during our monthly conversation.” 15. Employee in a New or Expanded Role “This was my first review period after taking on expanded responsibilities. I learned the new workflow, built relationships with key partners, and completed the initial deliverables agreed with my manager. Some goals changed as the role became clearer, and those revisions are documented in the goal record. My main development need is prioritizing requests from multiple stakeholders. In the next period, I will use an agreed priority framework, raise conflicts earlier, and review the approach with my manager after major planning meetings.” Blank Self-Evaluation Template The fields below mirror PerformSpark's free, downloadable employee self-appraisal template, available as an editable Word document and print-ready PDF if you would rather fill in a ready-made form than copy this structure by hand. Review-period context [Describe your role, review period, and any significant changes to responsibilities or priorities.] Major accomplishments [Describe two to four important contributions. For each, explain the objective, your role, evidence, and impact.] Goal progress [State the original target, current result, and relevant context for each important goal.] Feedback received and applied [Describe one or two pieces of feedback, the action you took, and what changed afterward.] Strengths [Describe observable behaviors or capabilities you should continue.] Development priorities [Describe one or two capabilities to build, why they matter, and the action you will take.] Next-period goals and support [List your next priorities and the manager or organizational support required.] Self-Evaluation Examples by Section Accomplishment “I owned [project or responsibility], completed [specific contribution], and used [evidence source] to confirm the result. The work helped [team, customer, process, or business impact].” Missed goal “I did not complete [goal] as planned. [Relevant context] affected the outcome, and I was responsible for [employee action or decision]. I have changed [specific behavior or process] and will review progress through [evidence and date].” Feedback applied “I received feedback that [observable behavior]. I responded by [action]. In the following [project or period], [evidence of change].” Development priority “I want to build [capability] because it will improve [current role or realistic next responsibility]. I will practice through [activity], and I need [manager support].” How Self-Evaluations Support the Review Process A self-evaluation adds the employee's perspective to the broader performance record. The manager should consider it alongside goals, project outcomes, feedback, survey information, recognition, and documented check-ins. When the organization uses performance calibration, relevant evidence from the employee may help the manager explain the proposed rating. Calibration still requires the complete evidence and rating standard. A strong self-evaluation does not guarantee a particular rating. Development priorities may move into an individual development plan. Current performance gaps may require coaching, clarified expectations, or a separate formal process after HR review. Common Self-Evaluation Mistakes Copying examples without adding real evidence Listing tasks instead of explaining contribution and impact Using invented percentages or financial results Claiming full credit for a team outcome Ignoring incomplete goals Using personality labels instead of behavior Creating a false weakness Writing only to argue for a rating Leaving out next steps and support Self-Evaluation Checklist The context and review period are clear. Examples represent the most important work. Evidence is accurate and available. Team and individual contributions are separated. Missed goals are addressed directly. Feedback includes the action taken. Development priorities are observable and actionable. Next goals include manager support. The final version uses clear US English. Use One Connected Review Record PerformSpark connects employee self-evaluations with manager assessments, goals, check-ins, recognition, feedback, calibration, development plans, and reporting. Explore PerformSpark pricing or book a personalized demo to see how employee and manager input can remain connected throughout the review cycle. Frequently Asked Questions What should a self-evaluation include? Include review-period context, major accomplishments, goal progress, feedback received and applied, relevant challenges, strengths, development priorities, next-period goals, and the manager or organizational support needed. How long should a self-evaluation be? There is no universal length. Follow the organization's questions and instructions. Use enough detail to support the most important accomplishments, goals, development priorities, and next steps without listing every task completed. How should an employee write about a missed goal? State the original expectation and result, explain relevant context, acknowledge the employee's responsibility, describe the corrective action, and define how progress will be reviewed. Do not hide the gap or accept responsibility for factors outside the employee's influence. Do self-evaluations determine performance ratings? No. A self-evaluation adds the employee's evidence and context to the review. The manager should consider it with goals, work outcomes, feedback, check-ins, and rating standards. The final rating should not be determined by the self-evaluation alone. What is the difference between a self-evaluation and a self-appraisal? The terms are commonly used interchangeably. Some organizations use self-evaluation for a written reflection and self-appraisal for an employee rating, but there is no universal distinction. Follow the terminology and format defined by the organization. How does calibration use self-evaluation information? Relevant self-evaluation evidence may help the manager explain a proposed rating during calibration. Participants should still review the complete performance record, role context, and rating definition. Employee statements do not replace manager judgment or determine the final rating. How can performance calibration software help reduce rating bias? Performance calibration software can support more consistent reviews by displaying manager ratings side by side, surfacing statistical outliers, and documenting the evidence discussed during calibration. A 9-box grid maps employees across two axes: performance and potential, placing each person into one of nine categories. What is rating normalization and why does it matter? Rating normalization is a structured review method for comparing how managers apply rating scales.
